A neighborhood house in a crowded industrial district cannot be content merely to distribute relief; its work is to establish a lasting relation between those who have leisure and those who have little. The residents who first took up quarters there expected to teach, and found themselves learning. They discovered that the families around them already possessed a deep practical wisdom — how to stretch a wage, how to nurse a sick child through a winter without heat — and that what they lacked was not character but opportunity. It followed that the proper business of the house was to open doors: to the library, to the night school, to the city council chamber where the questions of sanitation and street cleaning were settled. Charity of the old kind often left the giver comfortable and the receiver diminished; the newer practice asked both to sit at the same table.
